title: Hillel on the roof (Yoma 35b)
hook: too poor for the fee, young Hillel lay on the skylight in the snow to hear the lesson

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shammai's builder's rod, and the Talmud's lesson to be patient like Hillel. Your line was be patient like Hillel. Today, how Hillel himself learned.

Think of the last time you really wanted to be somewhere and couldn't afford it. A concert. A class. A trip your friends were taking. You stood outside it, in a way. Before Hillel was the great Hillel, he was a poor young man from Babylonia, working for tiny wages in Jerusalem. The best teachers in the city taught in a study house with a guard at the door and a fee to get in. One winter day he didn't have the fee. So what did he do?
screen: `OUTSIDE SOMETHING YOU WANTED.` → `A POOR YOUNG MAN IN JERUSALEM.` → `NO FEE TODAY.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, tractate Yoma. Every day Hillel worked and earned a small coin. Half went to the guard of the study house, where the teachers Shemaya and Avtalyon taught. Half fed his family. One day he earned nothing, and the guard wouldn't let him in. So Hillel climbed onto the roof and lay down by the skylight, to hear the words of the living God from their mouths. It was a Friday in the dead of winter, and snow began to fall. He stayed. The snow covered him. In the morning, Shemaya said to Avtalyon: my brother, every day this house is bright, and today it's dark. Is it cloudy? They looked up and saw the shape of a man in the skylight. They climbed up and found Hillel under a thick layer of snow. They brought him down, washed him, rubbed him with oil, and sat him by the fire, though it was Shabbat. This one, they said, is worth breaking the Sabbath for. Saving a life overrides Shabbat for anyone; the line is their way of saying how much they loved him. The Talmud tells the story for a reason. When poor people are asked why they didn't learn, it says, the answer comes back: were you poorer than Hillel? That's a hard question. But it isn't a scolding. It's an invitation. Learning finds a way in, even through the roof.
screen: `HALF FOR THE GUARD, HALF FOR HOME.` · `ONTO THE ROOF, BY THE SKYLIGHT.` · `THE HOUSE IS DARK TODAY.` · `WERE YOU POORER THAN HILLEL?` · then, large: `LISTEN THROUGH THE SNOW.`

segments.voice: Think of something you want to learn and keep putting off, a language, an instrument, a text, how to fix the thing that keeps breaking, and name the guard at its door: time, money, feeling too old, feeling behind. Now picture the skylight, one small way in anyway: a free library book, ten minutes before bed, a question to someone who knows. Hold that one way in.

Shemaya, one of the two teachers Hillel lay on a snowy skylight to hear. Too poor to pay the guard, Hillel listened from the roof, and Shemaya and his partner Avtalyon said he was worth breaking Shabbat for.
Your line: listen through the snow. Hillel found his way in from the roof. Two hundred seventy-four, done.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats Torah study as open to everyone, rich or poor, and the story of Hillel on the roof is often told to children and adults to show how much learning is worth.

notes: Yoma 35b paraphrased: Hillel's daily wage (a tropaik), half to the guard and half for his household, the skylight, Tevet snow (the Talmud says three cubits), Shemaya and Avtalyon, 'this one is worthy of desecrating Shabbat for'.
The script adds that saving a life overrides Shabbat for anyone, so the teachers' line is praise, not an exception; this follows standard commentary. Confirm the framing.
The 'were you poorer than Hillel' question is framed in the Talmud as a heavenly judgment; the script softens it to 'when poor people are asked'.
